reviews.basis: The reproduced original-page-4 recommendation seeks alignment with the Joint Office throughout implementation. Section 2.10 commits EPA and federal partners to continued engagement and monitoring, with referrals to section 2.9 and the final preamble. This supports broad coordination alignment, not a separate named MEMA disposition, complete alignment of regulations/priorities, or verified implementation.

MEMA asks EPA to follow through on critical-material, infrastructure and milestone assumptions and take action to realize them. The final preamble specifies data collection, reports and consultation about infrastructure and battery/material supply. EPA leaves later guidance, rulemaking or no change open. Monitoring is aligned with part of the request but is not a guarantee of all assumed outcomes or an automatic standards adjustment.

Original page 9 requests additional interstate infrastructure and increased hydrogen/DCFC funding targets. Section 2.10 commits coordination; sections 6.1 and 6.4 describe existing funding, freight-corridor planning and infrastructure investment. These passages do not establish a new allocation or increased funding target answering MEMA's request. They also do not establish no funding was awarded elsewhere.

PDF 875 reproduces the specific public-purchase recommendation from original page 10. PDF 987 separately reproduces its page-9/10 rationale, not the grant criterion. Section 6.4 names MEMA among future-proofing commenters, acknowledges potential V2G benefits and says those benefits were not quantitatively included in the rule analysis. Agreement with benefits and descriptions of existing programs do not verify adoption of a DCFC/bidirectional public-funding criterion.

The original-page-10 dashboard request is reproduced in section 6.1. That response promises periodic reports. The final preamble specifies collection and consultation but does not separately adopt the requested Joint Office dashboard in the compared passages. Section 6.4's public-information response begins by naming DTNA; its refusal of mandatory infrastructure reporting must not be recoded as a named refusal of MEMA's dashboard.

MEMA's original recommendation concerns national installation, operation and maintenance standards. The section-6.4 summary groups MEMA with MECA on minimum charger efficiency, while the reproduced MECA excerpt contains that specific efficiency request. The general responses cite FHWA's existing NEVI standards, reliability efforts and voluntary EnergyStar certification. These provide thematic context but do not separately establish full adoption of MEMA's broader lifecycle-standardization request.

The original-page-11 EV/EVSE cybersecurity recommendation and page-12 risk reference are reproduced. The complete section-6.1 and section-6.4 general responses discuss charging availability, reliability, efficiency and coordination without a separate disposition of this cybersecurity-policy request. Reliability or V2G national-security benefits are not a cybersecurity standard. This is bounded nonresolution, not docket-wide nonresponse.

The final adds a specified engagement, infrastructure/material monitoring and periodic-report commitment, with data collection stated for CY2025 and reports as early as CY2026. It preserves discretionary future action, not automatic adjustment. This is a scoped preamble comparison, not evidence MEMA originated or caused the commitment.
